messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Maid
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 64

She is forty-two, a South Asian woman who has spent most of her adult life cleaning other people’s homes. She leaves her apartment before sunrise with a tote bag of rags and sprays, moving quietly so she does not wake her husband. For years, the work suits her. She likes the order of it: beds made tight, counters wiped clean, floors shining. In the homes where she works, she is known as reliable, careful, and fast. She keeps to herself, listens more than she speaks, and takes pride in being someone others can trust with a key.

The trouble begins with a man in one of the apartment buildings where she cleans three units each week. At first, she notices him only because he seems to appear too often—in the lobby when she arrives, by the mailboxes when she leaves, standing outside smoking though he never seems to go anywhere. He smiles at her in a way that makes her uneasy. One morning he asks her name. She does not answer, only lowers her eyes and keeps walking. After that, he starts speaking to her as if they know each other. He comments on her clothes, asks what floor she is working on, tells her he has seen her around.

She tells herself not to make a big thing of it. Women learn to ignore men. But his presence grows harder to dismiss. He begins waiting near the service entrance. Twice she notices him following her when she leaves the building and walks to the bus stop. He stands too close. He tells her she is beautiful. He asks why she acts proud. One afternoon, while she is vacuuming, her phone buzzes with an unknown number. When she answers, there is silence at first, then his voice: “I know where you are.” She freezes in the empty living room, the sound of the vacuum still roaring in her hand.

After that, fear settles into her body. She starts checking behind her before unlocking any door. On the bus, she sits where she can see everyone getting on. She tells the building manager, who shrugs and says the man is “harmless” and maybe just lonely. She tells one of her employers, who offers sympathy but seems relieved it is not her problem. At home, she says little. Her husband tells her to ignore him, then later tells her maybe she should stop working in that building. She hears in his voice worry, but also frustration; they need the money.

The worst day comes in the late afternoon in winter, when darkness falls early. She finishes cleaning and steps into the parking area behind the building. He is there beside her car. She had not told anyone she drove that day. He says he has been waiting for her. He asks why she keeps avoiding him. When she tries to walk past, he grabs her wrist hard enough to leave bruises. She yanks free and screams. A delivery driver nearby turns his head, and the man lets go, smiling as if nothing has happened. She locks herself inside the car and cannot fit the key into the ignition because her hands are shaking so badly. For a long time afterward, she remembers most clearly not his words but the confidence in him, the sense that he believed he could reach into her life whenever he wanted.

She reports it to police. A statement is taken. There are questions she struggles to answer: how many times had she seen him, what exactly had he said, why had she not reported it earlier. She leaves feeling exposed and foolish. For several weeks she does not return to that building, then loses those clients altogether. Even after the police warn him, she still sees him—or thinks she does. A man in a gray jacket outside the grocery store. Footsteps behind her at dusk. A figure across the street as she pulls the curtains closed.

Now, months later, her world has become small. She still works, but only in houses where the owners are home or in buildings she already knows well. She calls her husband between jobs so he knows where she is. If an unknown number appears on her phone, her stomach drops. She no longer wears headphones while she cleans because she needs to hear every sound in the hallway. When she scrubs a bathroom sink, her mind suddenly flashes to the parking lot, to his hand around her wrist, and she has to stop and breathe against the edge of the counter until the room feels real again.

Sleep brings little relief. She wakes at slight noises and lies rigid, listening for footsteps outside the apartment door. Some nights she dreams that she opens a client’s front door and finds him already inside, sitting calmly at the kitchen table. In the morning she feels ashamed of how tired and irritable she is. Small things set her off: her husband coming up behind her, her niece teasing her for being “so jumpy,” a stranger looking too long in a queue. She used to enjoy talking with other women on the bus ride home; now she keeps her face turned to the window and watches every stop, counting the blocks, rehearsing what she will do if she sees him again.
